To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cancer patients in Pakistan have low levels of satisfaction with and perceptions of effectiveness for allopathy and high levels of satisfaction for traditional medicines and globalized complementary and alternatives.

cancer patients in Pakistan use both allopathic and traditional medicines and that their perceptions of the effectiveness of these medicines are not the same, although they do report high levels of satisfaction.
cancer patients’ perceptions of effectiveness of traditional medicine are low but their levels of satisfaction with traditional medicine are high.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the social and cultural processes underlying patients’ perceptions of effectiveness and levels of satisfaction with traditional medicines and allopaths for cancer care in the context of pluralistic medical environments in Pakistan.
the social processes that underlie the use of traditional medicine by cancer patients and their perceptions of the effectiveness and satisfaction with different forms of medicine.

the ways in which patients make sense of the pluralistic health care environment, and how their understandings of the effectiveness of different modalities are shaped by their own cultural and social contexts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cancer patients in Pakistan have a high degree of satisfaction with traditional medicines, which are used alongside allopathic medicines, for treating their cancer.
there are significant variations in the use of traditional medicines for cancer treatment in Pakistan, and that these variations are associated with different social and cultural factors.

the patients are satisfied with the traditional medicine and allopathic medicine for cancer care, but the patients’ perceptions of effectiveness and the satisfaction with traditional medicine for treating cancer is low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the patients’ preferences and perceptions of the different types of medicine were not uniform and that there was no single type of medicine that was perceived to be more effective or more satisfactory than others.
patients are not satisfied with the allopathic treatments for cancer and they are looking for alternative options to cure their diseases.
patients’ perceptions of traditional medicines for cancer care are not as low as one might expect.
The main takeaway from our work is that

patients’ perceptions of traditional medicine are not necessarily in conflict with their perceptions of allopathic cancer treatments, and that patients’ satisfaction with traditional medicine is high.
patients’ preferences for traditional and complementary medicine should be considered when planning and providing cancer care.

the pluralistic medical environment in Pakistan, with its diverse forms of complementary and alternative medicine and traditional medicine, provides a unique opportunity to study the social and cultural processes underlying the use of these medicines and the reasons why some forms of complementary and alternative medicine/traditional medicines are used more than others.
